name: Emergency preparedness trivia (medium)
description: 25 questions drawn only from Nimrod's fact-checked course Practical emergency preparedness at home; each cites a page the course cites. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Practical emergency preparedness at home (Nimrod course) and the pages it cites

items.question: If a fire breaks out at home, what does Class 1 say to do before calling 911?
answers: Get to a place of safety first
Dial 911 from the room where it started
Wait for the smoke alarm to repeat
Look for a landline to call from
items.correct: Get to a place of safety first
items.explain: Fire is the one exception to calling right away. Get to safety first, then call 911.

source.title: Know How and When to Contact 911

items.question: You realize you have called 911 by mistake. What does the course say to do?
answers: Hang up quickly to free the line
Stay on the line and say it was a mistake
Hang up and wait for a call back
Hang up and text 911 to explain
items.correct: Stay on the line and say it was a mistake
items.explain: Do not just hang up. If you hang up, 911 may have to call you back or send someone to check.

source.title: What Happens If You Call 911 and Hang Up?

items.question: According to the course, why does a 911 call-taker ask so many questions?
answers: To decide whether your call qualifies for a response
To choose the type and level of help to send
To check that you really need an ambulance
To fill in a form before help can be sent
items.correct: To choose the type and level of help to send
items.explain: The questions are not a test. They are used to choose the right type and level of help.

source.title: Why does the 911 call taker ask so many questions?

items.question: Alex is on a 911 call and cannot tell whether Sam is awake or breathing. What does the course say to do?
answers: Give the most likely guess
Say that you can't tell
Wait to answer until you are sure
Describe the whole story at length
items.correct: Say that you can't tell
items.explain: It is fine to say "I don't know" or "I can't tell." Do not guess or make something up.

source.title: Get the 411 on calling 911

items.question: When you text 911, what should come first in your message?
answers: Your name
Where you are
A short greeting
Which service you need
items.correct: Where you are
items.explain: A text does not tell the call center exactly where you are, so put your location first. Then say what is wrong and what help you need.

source.title: Text 911 (repeats FCC guidelines)

items.question: Where texting 911 is not offered, what does the FCC require to happen when you try?
answers: A call-taker phones you back within minutes
An automatic reply says your text did not go through
The text is saved until service is available
The text is forwarded to the nearest call center
items.correct: An automatic reply says your text did not go through
items.explain: The FCC requires a bounce-back message. It says the text did not go through and tells you to use another way, such as a voice call.

source.title: Text to 911: What You Need to Know

items.question: On the one-page medical sheet, what does "baseline" mean?
answers: The lowest dose of each medicine
The person's usual abilities, behaviour and signs
The first reading taken at the hospital
The date the page was last updated
items.correct: The person's usual abilities, behaviour and signs
items.explain: Baseline is what is usual for this person. It lets staff see what has changed.

source.title: Going to the Hospital: Tips for Dementia Caregivers (Alzheimer's Caregiving)

items.question: Where does the course suggest keeping copies of the one-page medical sheet?
answers: Only on your phone, to avoid losing paper
Only in the go-bag, so it stays together
On the fridge, in the go-bag, and as a photo on your phone
Only in the wallet of the person you care for
items.correct: On the fridge, in the go-bag, and as a photo on your phone
items.explain: Keep copies in more than one place. A copy with the emergency contact person also helps, so someone else can find it.

source.title: Emergency Preparedness for Children with Special Health Care Needs: Emergency Information Form instructions for parents

items.question: To tell your fire department that someone with a disability lives at your address, which number should you use?
answers: 911, so the call is logged
The fire department's non-emergency number
Any 911 text line in your area
The number of the nearest hospital
items.correct: The fire department's non-emergency number
items.explain: Look up the non-emergency number first. 911.gov says not to call 911 just to get a non-emergency number.

source.title: FAQ About Calling 911

items.question: According to the course, how many firefighters usually help someone out of a burning home?
answers: One firefighter
At least two firefighters
At least four firefighters
A full crew of six
items.correct: At least two firefighters
items.explain: At least two firefighters usually help someone out. If the agency knows early, it can call for backup.

source.title: Accessibility In Fire Emergencies

items.question: In Class 6, what does "blended" mean for a first aid class?
answers: Half video lessons and half written quiz
Online work plus a hands-on session
Two instructors teaching together
Adults and children in the same class
items.correct: Online work plus a hands-on session
items.explain: The Red Cross offers first aid training online, in person, and blended. Blended means online work plus a hands-on session.

source.title: First Aid Training

items.question: Why does the course say first-aid courses teach the side (recovery) position for a person who is unresponsive but breathing normally?
answers: It makes the person wake up sooner
It may lower the risk of a blocked airway and lets fluid drain
It helps the call-taker hear the person breathe
It keeps the person from getting too hot
items.correct: It may lower the risk of a blocked airway and lets fluid drain
items.explain: The AHA and Red Cross guidelines say this position may lower the risk of a blocked airway. It also lets fluid drain from the mouth.

source.title: 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid

items.question: For a baby who is choking, what do courses teach after the five firm back blows?
answers: Five abdominal thrusts
Five chest thrusts, with the baby face-up
Five more back blows
Hang the baby upside down
items.correct: Five chest thrusts, with the baby face-up
items.explain: For infants, courses teach five back blows, then five chest thrusts. Never abdominal thrusts.

source.title: Infant Choking: How To Help

items.question: Why does the Red Cross say its online-only classes fall short for first aid skills?
answers: They do not cover choking
They cost more than in-person classes
They are written only for children
They do not let you show your skills to an instructor
items.correct: They do not let you show your skills to an instructor
items.explain: This is why the course stresses a hands-on class, where you practise with an instructor.

source.title: Online Safety Classes & Training

items.question: After how many years from the manufacture date should a smoke alarm be replaced?
answers: 5 years
7 years
10 years
15 years
items.correct: 10 years
items.explain: Replace each smoke alarm 10 years after its manufacture date, which is printed on the back label.

source.title: Smoke Alarm Information (Learn More About Smoke Alarms)

items.question: During a power cut, where does the course say to use a generator?
answers: Outdoors, more than 20 feet from doors and windows
Outdoors, about 5 feet from the house wall
In the garage with the door open
In the basement near a window
items.correct: Outdoors, more than 20 feet from doors and windows
items.explain: Generators make carbon monoxide. Use one only outside, more than 20 feet from your home, doors and windows.

source.title: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning Prevention

items.question: During a fire, what does the Red Cross say about a door that feels warm to the back of your hand?
answers: Open it quickly and run through
Open it a little to check the hall
Do not open it; use another way out
Open it only if you have a flashlight
items.correct: Do not open it; use another way out
items.explain: Do not open a door that feels warm to the back of your hand. Use a second way out instead.

source.title: Fire Prevention Week: Install Smoke Alarms & Create Home Fire Escape Plan

items.question: How often does NFPA say to practise your home fire escape plan?
answers: Once a year
Twice a year
Every month
Only when the plan changes
items.correct: Twice a year
items.explain: NFPA says to practise twice a year and make the drill as realistic as possible. Practise again whenever the plan changes.

source.title: How to make a home fire escape plan

items.question: In a power cut, how long does a closed fridge keep food cold, according to the course?
answers: About one hour
About four hours
About twelve hours
About 48 hours
items.correct: About four hours
items.explain: A fridge keeps food cold for about four hours, and a full freezer about 48. Those figures are for food, so for medicine ask your pharmacist.

source.title: Power Outages (Ready Kids)

items.question: Why must you never plug a generator into a wall outlet or the house wiring?
answers: The current can flow back into power lines and endanger utility workers
It can overload the generator's fuel tank
It makes the generator louder
It voids the generator's warranty
items.correct: The current can flow back into power lines and endanger utility workers
items.explain: Plug devices directly into the generator instead. Ask a licensed electrician or your utility about safe hookups.

source.title: How to safely use a generator during a power outage (reporting CDC advice)

items.question: How often does the CDC say to check your emergency kit so the contents are current and working?
answers: Every month
Every 6 months
Once every two years
Only after using it
items.correct: Every 6 months
items.explain: Check kits every 6 months. Replace old food, water, medicines and batteries.

source.title: Building an Emergency Kit

items.question: What does a winter storm watch mean?
answers: Dangerous winter weather is possible, so get ready
Dangerous winter weather is imminent
A less severe event, but travel may still be dangerous
The storm has passed and roads are clearing
items.correct: Dangerous winter weather is possible, so get ready
items.explain: A watch usually comes first, about 12 to 36 hours ahead. A warning means the dangerous weather is imminent.

source.title: Winter Weather (watches, warnings, advisories)

items.question: What does Ready.gov say about relying on a fan during extreme heat?
answers: A fan lowers body temperature enough to replace cooling
A fan is the best main cooling during a power cut
A fan creates airflow and false comfort but does not reduce body temperature
A fan cools a closed room by several degrees
items.correct: A fan creates airflow and false comfort but does not reduce body temperature
items.explain: Do not rely on a fan as your main cooling. A fan moves air; it does not cool the room.

source.title: Extreme Heat

items.question: If a phone call fails during a crisis, how long does the course say to wait before redialing?
answers: Redial immediately
10 seconds
1 minute
30 minutes
items.correct: 10 seconds
items.explain: Redialing too fast adds to the jam. You can also try a text, email, or a landline.

source.title: Tips for Communicating in an Emergency

items.question: If your electric company has a priority list or medical registry, what does the checklist say about backup power?
answers: Keep your own backup, because a registry does not promise power
The registry will restore your power first
You can skip a backup plan once registered
A registry replaces the need for a power plan
items.correct: Keep your own backup, because a registry does not promise power
items.explain: A registry means you tell the company about your needs. You still plan your own batteries or other power.

source.title: Emergency Power Planning for People Who Use Electricity and Battery-Dependent Assistive Technology and Medical Devices
